text: You're never taller than when you look up.
explanation:
With five loaves, two small fish and thousands of hungry people in front of Him, Jesus "looked up to heaven, and blessed." That's the posture God made us for. The enemy wants you looking around: comparing, competing, envying. When Peter asked about John, Jesus said, "What is that to you? You follow Me."

Looking up is true humility. It says, "I can't, but He can." Keep your eyes on the exalted Man at the Father's right hand, who holds all authority in heaven and on earth. You're never more frightening to the devil than when you look up.

text: Who will be caught up? Not "we who are faithful" or "we who are overcomers," but "we who are alive and remain."
explanation:
Picture a young believer in Thessalonica, one who sometimes wins against temptation and sometimes loses, listening anxiously as Paul's letter is read aloud. "For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who…" Who? The faithful? The watchful? "…we who are alive and remain."

The rapture is the redemption of your body, and your body is redeemed by the same grace that saved your soul: not half grace and half your performance. Live to honour Him, yes. But the Lord is coming to claim what He already purchased, and He paid for all of you.

text: Paul wrote "We shall all be changed" to the most carnal church he ever had: the Corinthians.
explanation:
The Corinthian believers were suing one another, splitting into factions and abusing the Lord's Supper, yet Paul called their bodies temples of the Holy Spirit. And to them he wrote, "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment." All. The order of resurrection is "Christ the firstfruits, afterward those who are Christ's at His coming": those who belong to Him.

That isn't a licence to live carelessly; a believer living in sin is a walking civil war. But fear never produced lasting holiness. "Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself." It's the blessed hope that cleans you up.

text: "I'm not afraid of the bulldozers. He said that when my new house was ready, he'd come for me himself."
explanation:
A landowner bought a large estate for development, with an old woman's run-down cottage in the middle of it. He visited her personally and promised her a much better house, with running water and help close by: "When it's ready, I'll come and get you myself." Months later, the bulldozers lined up outside her door. A worker asked if she was frightened. "No," she said. "He told me he's coming for me." And he did.

As you watch the world's troubles gather, remember who promised, "I go to prepare a place for you… I will come again and receive you to Myself." The worst hasn't happened yet, and He's coming for you first.

text: Luke begins with a priest who came out of the temple unable to bless. It ends with our High Priest ascending with His hands raised in blessing.
explanation:
In Luke 1, the people waited outside while Zacharias burned incense in the temple, wondering why he was taking so long. When he finally came out, he'd been struck mute and couldn't pronounce the priestly blessing. Nothing is sadder than a priest who can't bless.

Luke's Gospel closes with Jesus lifting His hands to bless His disciples, "and while He blessed them, He was parted from them." Now He has gone into the true Holy Place, and "to those who eagerly wait for Him He will appear a second time." Waiting isn't a condition you must meet; it's what His people naturally do while their Priest is inside. And when He comes out, He'll come out blessing.

text: The Old Testament ends with the Sun of Righteousness. The New ends with the Bright and Morning Star, which rises before the sun.
explanation:
The last chapter of the Old Testament promises Israel that "the Sun of Righteousness shall arise with healing in His wings." The last chapter of the Bible has Jesus calling Himself "the Bright and Morning Star." The morning star appears in the dark, before the dawn; only later does the sun rise for the day.

That's a picture of the two stages of His coming: first for His church, quietly and suddenly, before the day of judgment; then in full brightness for Israel and the world. Jesus' last words in Scripture are "Surely I am coming quickly," and the church answers, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus!"
